topics.title: Mc states 17
topics.text:
A number is the product of a prime and a perfect square. It is also the product of a different prime and a perfect cube. What is the lowest  possible value of this number?

my solMy take: The two different primes should be 2 and 3 to minimize the product. Hence, the prime factorization of the answer should be of entirely 2s and 3s. Hence:

$2^m3^n = 2 *2^{m-1}3^n = 3 * 2^m3^{n - 
1}$ 2 should be the prime that is to be multiplied by the perfect cube (for minimization) and 3 the  perfect square. It follows that $m-1$ must be divisible by 3, so the lowest value of $m$ is 4. $n$ must also be divisib by 3, making the lowest value of $n$ to be 3. Note that for the third expression to work, $n - 1$ and $m$ must be even, which they already are. so answer is $16 x 27 = 432$

topics.title: 2016 AMC 8 Problem 16
topics.text:
Hello. While I was practicing for next years AMC 8 (mathcounts,  jr. high mathleague, and other contests) competition, I was solving previous years' AMC 8 competition problems. I came across 2016 AMC 8 Problem 16 and noticed an explanation flaw (the Aops explanation, to clarify (I do not know whether or not there is a difference) (I do agree with the answer, though). Here is my calculus: From the explanation, "Each lap Bonnie runs, Annie runs another quarter lap, so Bonnie will run four laps before she is overtaken. This means that Annie and Bonnie are equal so that Annie need to run [Here is a grammar error, too] another lap to overtake Bonnie." I do not agree with the last sentence, for infinitesimally after that instant, Annie will have run an infinitesimal distance, thereby, passing Bonnie.



I think a better explanation would be the following: Per Bonnie's one lap, Annie runs 1.25 laps. One can subtract 1 from both of the speeds to get 0 laps per 0.25 laps. Annie will reach Bonnie when she reaches 1 lap (she will, therefore, cycle around four times). Thus, 4*1.25 = 5. Finally, infinitesimally after Annie reaches Bonnie, Annie will have traveled an infinitesimal distance, hence, passing her.



Is there really an explanation flaw (i.e. is my calculus fallacious)? Furthermore, is my explanation correct? I appreciate the feedback.

topics.title: k Does 1 =2
topics.text:
Just some thought I was thinking about. [Can 1=2?]



If we start off with $a=b$ then multiply both sides by $a$



$a^2=ab$



then subtract both sides by $b^2$.



We get, $a^2 - b^2 = ab - b^2$.



If we factor from both sides, we get



$(a + b)(a - b) = b(a - b)$



Solving, we get $a+b=b$.



Since $a=b$ (make $a$ = $b$), then we can solidly confirm that



$b+b=b$



$2b=b$



Hence, $2=1$

topics.title: Math Challenge Problem
topics.text:
A right triangle, triangle ABC, is constructed so that its base, AB, is twice its height,

BC. That is, AB = 2BC.

A square is constructed in the following way:

• one vertex is at B;

• a second vertex is at D, somewhere on

AB between A and B;

• a third vertex is at F, somewhere on

BC between B and C; and

• the final vertex E lies on the hypotenuse

AC, between A and C.



This square, DEFB is called an inscribed square. Determine the ratio of the

area of the inscribed square DEFB to triangle ABC.
